title: A Point Sliding Along an Arc
statement: Two circles of equal radius have centres $A$ and $B$. The circle centred at $A$ passes through $B$, and the circle centred at $B$ passes through $A$. Let $E$ be one of the two points where the circles intersect. The line $AB$ meets the circle centred at $A$ at $B$ and at a second point $C$. A point $P$ moves along the arc $CE$ of the circle centred at $A$ that does not contain $B$, and $P$ is never equal to $C$ or $E$. How many different integer values can the degree measure of $\angle BEP$ take?
hints: Draw the radii $AE$ and $AP$. What kind of triangle is $ABE$, and what kind is $AEP$?

Use angle chasing. Triangle $ABE$ has three sides equal to the common radius, and triangle $AEP$ is isosceles because $AE = AP$. Split $\angle BEP$ along the ray $EA$ into $\angle BEA$ and $\angle AEP$.

Let $\theta = \angle EAP$. Then $\theta$ can be any value strictly between $0^\circ$ and $120^\circ$, and $\angle AEP = 90^\circ - \frac{\theta}{2}$. Adding $\angle BEA = 60^\circ$ shows that $\angle BEP$ takes every value strictly between $90^\circ$ and $150^\circ$. It remains to count the integers in this range.
solution: Each of $AB$, $AE$ and $BE$ is a radius of one of the two equal circles, so triangle $ABE$ is equilateral and $\angle BEA = \angle BAE = 60^\circ$. Since $BC$ is a diameter of the circle centred at $A$, the point $A$ lies between $B$ and $C$, so $\angle EAC = 180^\circ - 60^\circ = 120^\circ$. Thus the arc $CE$ not containing $B$ has central angle $120^\circ$. As $P$ moves along this arc, excluding its endpoints, $\theta = \angle EAP$ takes every value strictly between $0^\circ$ and $120^\circ$. Since $AE = AP$, triangle $AEP$ is isosceles with apex angle $\theta$. Its base angles are equal and the angles of the triangle sum to $180^\circ$, so $\angle AEP = 90^\circ - \frac{\theta}{2}$. Next we show that the angles at $E$ add. The points $B$ and $C$ lie on opposite sides of line $AE$, because segment $BC$ crosses that line at $A$. The arc from $E$ to $C$ has central angle less than $180^\circ$, so apart from $E$ it does not meet line $AE$ and stays on the same side as $C$. Hence $P$ and $B$ lie on opposite sides of line $AE$. Also $\angle BEA + \angle AEP = 60^\circ + 90^\circ - \frac{\theta}{2} < 180^\circ$, so the ray $EA$ lies inside $\angle BEP$. Therefore $$\angle BEP = 60^\circ + 90^\circ - \dfrac{\theta}{2} = 150^\circ - \dfrac{\theta}{2}.$$ As $\theta$ takes every value strictly between $0^\circ$ and $120^\circ$, the quantity $150^\circ - \frac{\theta}{2}$ takes every value strictly between $90^\circ$ and $150^\circ$, and no others. The integer degree values are therefore $91, 92, \ldots, 149$, and there are $149 - 91 + 1 = 59$ of them. The answer is $59$. Why this works. angle-chasing, two-intersecting-circles: equal radii fix an equilateral triangle and an isosceles triangle, which turn $\angle BEP$ into a simple function of the central angle at $A$.

solution_figures.alt: Two equal circles with centres A and B, each passing through the other's centre, meet at E. C is the second point where line AB meets the circle centred at A, and P lies on arc CE away from B. Triangle ABE is equilateral with a 60 degree angle at E, triangle AEP is isosceles with AE = AP and apex angle theta at A, and segment EP is highlighted.
